questions.questionText: What's the key structural difference between LangChain's classic AgentExecutor and LangGraph?
options: LangGraph doesn't support tools at all
LangGraph makes the control flow an explicit, inspectable graph of nodes and edges instead of a hidden loop
AgentExecutor is faster in every case
There is no real difference between them
questions.correctAnswer: LangGraph makes the control flow an explicit, inspectable graph of nodes and edges instead of a hidden loop
questions.explanation: AgentExecutor runs the ReAct loop as a black box; LangGraph exposes the same loop as nodes and edges you define, inspect, and modify yourself.

questions.questionText: What's the difference between a normal edge and a conditional edge in LangGraph?
options: There is no difference, they behave identically
A normal edge always goes to the same next node; a conditional edge picks the next node based on the current state
Conditional edges can only be used with tool nodes
Normal edges are only used for the START node
questions.correctAnswer: A normal edge always goes to the same next node; a conditional edge picks the next node based on the current state
questions.explanation: Conditional edges are what let a graph branch — e.g. routing to a tool node vs. END based on whether the agent's last message included a tool call.

questions.questionText: In the example code, what does a node function receive and return?
options: It receives nothing and returns a fixed string
It receives the current state and returns updates to that state
It receives the entire graph definition and returns a new graph
It receives only the user's original message, never the full state
questions.correctAnswer: It receives the current state and returns updates to that state
questions.explanation: Every node is a function of (state) -> partial state update — the agent node, for example, receives the message history and returns the new message to append.
